title: Japan’s New CIA Could Be Takaichi’s Trump Card
gist: Derek Grossman argues Japan under PM Takaichi is building its first foreign HUMINT service (a 'Japanese CIA') by 2028, following May legislation creating a National Intelligence Council and a 700-person National Intelligence Bureau, as a burden-sharing showcase for Trump and a path toward Five Eyes integration, though operational capability will take years.

insights.claim: Japan is undertaking its most substantial intelligence overhaul since 1945, aiming to create its own CIA-like foreign HUMINT agency by 2028 targeting China, North Korea and Russia.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Signals durable Japanese security normalization and alliance deepening.
insights.quote: with the ultimate goal of creating something Japan has never had: its own version of the CIA by 2028
insights.locator: When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi

insights.claim: In May Japan's parliament created a cabinet-level National Intelligence Council chaired by the PM and a National Intelligence Bureau that replaced the Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office and already has roughly 700 personnel.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Institutional groundwork makes the reform credible rather than rhetorical.
insights.quote: It is already operational with roughly 700 personnel

insights.claim: The government may expand the foreign ministry's 2015 Counter Terrorism Unit-Japan beyond terrorism into general national security HUMINT.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Likely institutional vehicle for the new agency.

insights.claim: Japan has strong SIGINT and satellite capabilities, but cases like North Korea's abductions show technical collection cannot reveal intentions, motivating HUMINT.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Explains the strategic logic behind the reform.
insights.quote: Satellites can photograph missile facilities, and signals intelligence can intercept communications

insights.claim: The intelligence reform is part of Japan's broader push to be a more self-reliant ally, alongside April's significant loosening of arms export restrictions to allow lethal weapons sales.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Arms-export liberalization opens growth for Japanese defense industry and US-Japan co-production.
insights.quote: Takaichi’s government significantly loosened Japan’s long-standing restrictions on arms exports

insights.claim: Japan could move toward deeper Five Eyes integration, possibly following the Australian model of a central coordinating body plus a separate foreign-ministry HUMINT agency, with Australia's ambassador Andrew Shearer advising.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Deeper allied intelligence integration strengthens Japan's role in Indo-Pacific deterrence.

insights.claim: Building an effective Japanese CIA will take years beyond its legal creation, needing case officers, cover, agent protection, a risk-tolerant culture and resolution of legal questions such as paying agents and nonofficial cover.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Near-term operational impact is limited; the signal is political rather than capability.
insights.quote: creating a Japanese CIA on paper will be far easier than building one capable of operating effectively overseas
